subject: ventures/chrome-extension-permission-check
professional: a Chrome extension developer who has shipped several MV3 extensions through Chrome Web Store review (first check: does the tool agree with Chrome's own permissions list on which APIs need a manifest permission, and does it ignore comments and strings)

evidence.correctness: Ran the CLI (node check.mjs) on fixtures in the scratchpad and recomputed against Chrome's own docs, fetched 2026-11-08 (HTTP 200): developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/permissions-list, /docs/extensions/reference/api/tabs, /docs/webstore/troubleshooting. (1) Fixture manifest permissions [storage], source calls chrome.tabs.create(...). Tool prints '[!] Tabs (tabs) -- detected-undeclared ... this will fail at runtime'. Chrome's tabs page: 'Most features don't require any permissions to use. For example: creating a new tab, reloading a tab, navigating...'; permissions list: 'tabs ... You usually don't need to declare this permission to use those APIs.' Tool is WRONG. (2) Source calls chrome.action.setBadgeText with no 'action' permission: tool prints '[!] Toolbar action (action) -- detected-undeclared ... will fail at runtime'. 'action' does not appear among the permission IDs in the permissions list (activeTab, alarms, audio, background, ...), and troubleshooting says action APIs 'do not need activeTab to function'. Tool is WRONG, and a CI gate on exit code forces users to add a non-existent permission. (3) Fixture with '// chrome.bookmarks.getTree()' and a string "chrome.alarms.create" with bookmarks and alarms declared: tool reports both '[OK] declared-and-detected' (comments and string literals count as usage), so an unused permission is hidden; a call split over two lines ('chrome.\n  tabs.query') is missed. (4) Correct: chrome.storage.local.set with storage declared gave OK; declared tabs+storage with only storage used gave declared-unused; host_permissions <all_urls> flagged broad (matches docs that storage/alarms/scripting etc. map to same-named permissions). Outputs for plain namespace permissions (storage, alarms, bookmarks, cookies...) match Chrome's list; the two most common namespaces (tabs, action) are wrong in the 'undeclared' direction. Tests run: 60 pass.
evidence.completeness: Claimed features checked by running: CLI with path, --manifest, --json (all worked); exit 0/1 gate (worked: exit 1 on undeclared/unused, 0 when clean); recursion with skip of node_modules/dist/build/out/coverage/.output/vendor/dotdirs (test and manual run OK); additional manifests noted not read (printed); declared-unused, detected-undeclared, broad host, uncheckable list and unmapped list (all printed); MV2 inline host patterns in permissions[] split out (parseManifest, tested); browser page index.html with file picker (page.test.mjs structure tests pass; not run in a real browser by this audit); four static pages exist (index, purple-potassium, two vs- pages) plus llms.txt, sitemap, robots. No stubs or TODOs found. Gaps: permissions list has about 70 IDs, the tool maps 49 and treats 20 or so valid ones (readingList, userScripts, search, tabGroups, favicon, printing, webRequestBlocking, dns, runtime for native messaging, ...) as 'no signature yet', which the README admits. llms.txt links point at the retired duncan-haywood.github.io host, not marisstella.app.
evidence.verification: cd ventures/chrome-extension-permission-check && node --test '*.test.mjs': 60 tests, 60 pass, 0 fail. Seeded three mutations in scan.mjs, one at a time, each reverted (git status clean afterwards, 60/60 pass again): (a) removed '<all_urls>' from BROAD_HOST_PATTERNS -> 2 tests failed (caught); (b) changed the declared-unused status to 'declared-and-detected' -> 4 failed (caught); (c) removed 'declaredUnusedCount === 0 &&' from report.ok -> 1 failed (caught). So the tests do guard the logic as the author understood it. Weakness: they encode the author's wrong belief, e.g. scan.test.mjs lines 104-109 and 159-167 assert chrome.tabs.query without 'tabs' is detected-undeclared, which Chrome's docs contradict; nothing tests comments, string literals, multi-line calls, or a chrome.action-only extension. Tests also check that pages contain the disclaimer, but only structure, not the permission map against any external list.
evidence.craft: Read scan.mjs (203 lines), check.mjs (about 190), usage.mjs (65), check.test.mjs, scan.test.mjs. Positives: pure functions separate from I/O, browser and CLI share one module, usage counter wraps storage in try/catch and keeps opt-out in its own key, no network calls, clear comments. Defects: detection is a per-line regex over raw text with no comment or string stripping (false 'used'), no multi-line handling; the first manifest.json found is read silently apart from a note, and walk order is directory order so which manifest wins is arbitrary in a monorepo; a missing --manifest file yields an empty manifest with parseNote 'file not found' but the run then reports every detected API as undeclared rather than a hard error; a manifest.json that is invalid JSON in the tree yields a report whose only signal is a parseNote; SOURCE_EXTENSIONS omits .vue/.svelte/.html inline scripts, and HTML-embedded scripts (popup.html) are not scanned though extensions commonly use them; permission-to-API model conflates 'namespace exists' with 'permission required'.
evidence.claims: Checked: (1) README/index.html/VENTURE.yaml/purple-potassium page: Google's documentation 'names this the single most common review rejection reason'. troubleshooting page (fetched) lists 'requesting a permission but not using it' as a reason under Purple Potassium but contains no statement that it is the most common (grep of 'most common' finds only unrelated image-file text). UNBACKED, repeated in the page's FAQPage JSON-LD and meta text. (2) Output text 'will fail at runtime' for chrome.tabs and chrome.action without a permission: FALSE per Chrome docs. (3) UNCHECKABLE_PERMISSIONS 'background' described as 'lets the service worker be woken for background events'; the permissions list says it makes Chrome start early and shut down late. WRONG. (4) scan.mjs comment says Purple Potassium covers overly broad host access; the troubleshooting page text for that policy does not mention it (low). (5) 'Nothing is uploaded / CLI never makes network call': backed by reading the code (no fetch, no network imports). (6) MIT LICENSE exists, no-warranty and not-affiliated-with-Google text present, and the 'Evidence, not a determination' framing is honest. (7) llms.txt URLs point to the old github.io host (low). Three of the claims a developer would act on are not backed by Google's documentation.
evidence.fitness: Job walked through: a developer about to submit an MV3 extension runs node check.mjs . and acts on the report. For a typical extension that calls chrome.tabs.* and chrome.action.* with the usual manifest (no 'action' permission, no 'tabs'), the report fails the gate and tells them to add 'action' (not a valid permission) and 'tabs' (which adds the 'Read your browsing history' install warning, making the extension MORE likely to be questioned under Purple Potassium). The unused-direction check works for plain namespaces (storage, alarms, bookmarks, cookies, notifications) and that is the tool's headline job, so a developer can still find a genuinely unused permission; but they must discount two of the most common findings and cannot trust the exit code as a CI gate without a workaround. No way to suppress or allowlist a finding.
evidence.domain: Compared against Chrome's permissions list and the tabs API page (the reference a Web Store reviewer and an extension developer use) and the Purple Potassium section of the troubleshooting page. Departures: treats chrome.tabs and chrome.action as permission-gated (they are not); describes 'background' incorrectly; does not model that the 'tabs' permission only gates the url, pendingUrl, title and favIconUrl properties, so it cannot say when 'tabs' is genuinely needed or unneeded, which is the specific misunderstanding the troubleshooting page warns about; does not model that 'runtime' permission means only connectNative/sendNativeMessage (it does map nativeMessaging calls but flags the ID 'nativeMessaging' only, which is right) and omits host-permission-needs-for-scripting/webRequest. The core idea (cross-check declared against used) is what reviewers do, so a practitioner would like the premise but would not sign off on the permission model.

defects.what: chrome.action.* usage is reported 'detected-undeclared ... will fail at runtime' unless an 'action' permission is declared, but 'action' is not a manifest permission (absent from Chrome's permissions list). Any MV3 extension with a toolbar action fails the CI gate and is told to add an invalid permission.

chrome.tabs.* usage without a 'tabs' permission is reported as a runtime failure; Chrome's docs say most tabs APIs (create, reload, update, query of current tab, sendMessage) need no permission, and 'tabs' only exposes url/pendingUrl/title/favIconUrl. False positive on the most common namespace, and the tests assert the wrong behaviour.

Detection runs on raw lines with no comment or string stripping: '// chrome.bookmarks.getTree()' or a string literal counts as use, hiding a genuinely unused permission (the tool's headline claim). Calls split across lines are missed.

Claim that Google's documentation names unused permissions 'the single most common review rejection reason' is not in the cited troubleshooting page; it is repeated in README, VENTURE.yaml, meta/FAQ JSON-LD of index.html and the purple-potassium page.
'background' permission is described as waking the service worker; Chrome's list says it makes Chrome start at login and stay running after the last window closes.
Inline scripts in .html files (popup.html, options.html) are not scanned, and .vue/.svelte are skipped, so permissions used only there read as unused.
llms.txt links to the retired duncan-haywood.github.io host; boilerplate says 'estimates from the numbers typed in', which does not fit a scanner.

verdict: Does not meet the bar and is finished only in the sense that every advertised feature runs. It is a tidy, dependency-free 60-test scanner whose tests catch seeded bugs (3 of 3 mutations caught), and its unused-permission direction is right for plain namespaces such as storage, alarms and bookmarks. But checked against Chrome's own permissions list and tabs API page, it wrongly reports chrome.tabs and chrome.action usage as runtime failures when no 'tabs' or 'action' permission is declared (the latter does not exist as a permission), so the exit-code gate fails ordinary MV3 extensions; comments and strings count as usage; and the headline claim that Google calls this the single most common rejection reason is not in the cited page. Correctness 1, claims 1, domain 1. Fix: remove action from PERMISSION_SIGNATURES, drop 'tabs' from the undeclared check (or only flag it when tab.url/title are read), strip comments and strings before matching, correct the 'most common' claim and the 'background' text.
